original_value: AbstractMotivationGene set testing, or pathway analysis, has become a critical tool for the analysis of high-dimensional genomic data. Although the function and activity of many genes and higher-level processes is tissue-specific, gene set testing is typically performed in a tissue agnostic fashion, which impacts statistical power and the interpretation and replication of results.ResultsTo address this challenge, we have developed a bioinformatics approach to compute tissue-specific weights for individual gene sets using information on tissue-specific gene activity from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). We used this approach to create a public repository of tissue-specific gene set weights for 37 different human tissue types from the HPA and all collections in the Molecular Signatures Database. To demonstrate the validity and utility of these weights, we explored three different applications: the functional characterization of human tissues, multi-tissue analysis for systemic diseases and tissue-specific gene set testing.Availability and implementationAll data used in the reported analyses is publicly available. An R implementation of the method and tissue-specific weights for MSigDB gene set collections can be downloaded at http://www.dartmouth.edu/∼hrfrost/TissueSpecificGeneSets.

result.paraphrase: AbstractMotivationGene set testing, also called pathway analysis, has become an important method for analyzing high-dimensional genomic data. Even though many genes and higher-level processes are tissue-specific in function and activity, gene set testing is usually carried out in a tissue-agnostic way, reducing statistical power and affecting how results are interpreted and replicated.ResultsTo meet this challenge, we developed a bioinformatics approach that calculates tissue-specific weights for individual gene sets using tissue-specific gene activity information from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). Using this method, we built a public repository of tissue-specific gene set weights for 37 human tissue types drawn from the HPA and all collections in the Molecular Signatures Database. To show the validity and usefulness of these weights, we examined three applications: functional characterization of human tissues, multi-tissue analysis of systemic diseases, and tissue-specific gene set testing.Availability and implementationAll data used in the analyses reported here are publicly available. An R implementation of the method, along with tissue-specific weights for MSigDB gene set collections, can be downloaded at http://www.dartmouth.edu/∼hrfrost/TissueSpecificGeneSets.
